chapter.title: Reading a shop in five numbers

cards.body:
Which is the bigger shop: one selling slices at ₹3,000, or one selling them at ₹50? In the bazaar, a share's price is just the cost of one slice. It tells you nothing about how big the shop is or how much it earns.

**A price only means something next to two other numbers: the size of the whole shop, and the profit it makes.**
cards.simpler: Which shop is bigger: one that sells slices at ₹3,000, or one that sells them at ₹50? You can't tell from that. A share's price is only the cost of one slice of a company. It says nothing about how big the shop is or how much money it makes. **A price only means something next to two other numbers: the size of the whole shop, and the profit it makes.**

cards.prompt: Two shops on the same lane. One slice of Lamp Ltd costs ₹3,000. One slice of Chai Co costs ₹50. Which shop is bigger?

options.text: Lamp Ltd. Its slice costs 60 times more.
Chai Co. Cheap slices must mean lots of customers.
You can't tell yet. You need to know how many slices each shop is cut into.

whyNot.a: That's the price of one slice, not the size of the shop. A pricey slice can come from a small shop cut into only a few pieces.
whyNot.b: That's a guess about popularity, not size. A low price per slice says nothing about how many slices exist.

cards.reteach: Knowing the price of one slice is like knowing the price of one brick. You still can't tell how big the building is until you know how many bricks went into it. Price times the number of shares gives you the size.

cards.title: Price is a slice. Market cap is the shop.
cards.body:
The *price* is what one share costs right now. On its own, it's one brick with no building around it.

*Market cap* is the price times every share the company has issued. Picture **the price tag on the whole shop**, as if someone bought every slice at today's price. In India it's shown in crore (1 crore is 1,00,00,000 rupees).

SEBI sorts companies by market cap. The top 100 count as *large cap*, the next 150 as *mid cap*, and everything after that as *small cap*. So the size label on your quote page comes from this one sum, not from the share price.
cards.simpler: The price is what one share costs today. Market cap is that price times every share the company has. Think of it as **the price tag on the whole shop**, as if you bought every slice today. In India it's shown in crore, and 1 crore is 1,00,00,000 rupees. SEBI sorts companies by market cap. The top 100 are large cap, the next 150 mid cap, the rest small cap. That size label comes from market cap, not share price.

cards.title: The ₹3,000 shop is the small one
cards.body:
Two made-up shops. Chai Co costs ₹50 a share and has 200 crore shares, so its market cap is ₹10,000 crore. Lamp Ltd costs ₹3,000 a share but has only 2 crore shares, so its market cap is ₹6,000 crore.

The shop with the scary price tag is the smaller one, by **₹4,000 crore**. Lamp Ltd just cut itself into fewer, chunkier slices.
cards.simpler: Take two made-up shops. Chai Co sells shares at ₹50 and has 200 crore of them, so the whole shop is worth ₹10,000 crore. Lamp Ltd sells shares at ₹3,000 but has only 2 crore of them, so it's worth ₹6,000 crore. The shop with the scary price is the smaller one, by **₹4,000 crore**. Lamp Ltd cut itself into fewer, bigger slices, like a cake cut into four pieces instead of forty.

cards.prompt: A share on your app costs ₹1,20,000. Your cousin says that makes it one of India's biggest companies. What do you check?

options.text: The market cap on the quote page: the price times all its shares.
Nothing. Any share above ₹1 lakh belongs to a large company.
How much the price moved today.

whyNot.b: That's the cost of one slice, not the shop. A few very expensive slices can still add up to a small shop.
whyNot.c: That's today's buyers and sellers from chapter 1, not the size of the shop.

cards.reteach: Size is the price times the number of shares. A ₹1,20,000 share in a company with only a few lakh shares can be smaller than a ₹100 share in a company with crores of shares. The quote page does this sum for you on the market cap line.

cards.title: Price against profit
cards.body:
Market cap tells you whether a shop is big or small, but not whether its shares are pricey or cheap. For that you use *P/E*: the share price divided by the yearly profit each share earns. Read it as **how many years of today's profit you're paying for**.

Back on our lane: Chai Co earns ₹1 a share each year, so its P/E is 50. Lamp Ltd earns ₹150 a share, so its P/E is 20. The ₹3,000 slice is cheaper against its profit. That alone doesn't make it the better buy, because growth and risk matter too.
cards.simpler: Market cap shows size, not whether a share is cheap. For that, use P/E: price divided by yearly profit per share. It tells you **how many years of today's profit you're paying for**. Chai Co earns ₹1 a share, so its P/E is 50. Lamp Ltd earns ₹150, so its P/E is 20: cheaper against its profit. That doesn't make it the better buy on its own, because growth and risk matter too.

cards.body: Anjali spots a share at ₹14 and buys 500 because 'it's so cheap.' She never opened the quote page, where the P/E was 90. She'd paid for about 90 years of the shop's current profit. **A low price is not a low valuation.** Before you call anything cheap, check the P/E, not the price tag.
cards.simpler: Anjali sees a share at ₹14 and buys 500, because it looks so cheap. She never opened the quote page, where the P/E was 90. That means she paid for about 90 years of the shop's profit, if that profit stayed the same. **A low price is not the same as a cheap share.** Before you call anything cheap, check the P/E, not the price tag.

cards.prompt: Shop X: price ₹200, profit ₹20 per share a year. Shop Y: price ₹900, profit ₹90 per share a year. Measured against profit, which is pricier?

options.text: Shop Y. Its price is 4.5 times higher.
Shop X. Its profit is smaller.
Neither. Both have a P/E of 10.

whyNot.a: That's the price tag, not the price against profit. Divide 900 by 90 and you get 10, same as X.
whyNot.b: That's the profit on its own, not the ratio. ₹200 for ₹20 a year is 10 years, same as Y.

cards.reteach: P/E is the price divided by yearly profit per share. For X, 200 ÷ 20 = 10. For Y, 900 ÷ 90 = 10. Both cost you 10 years of today's profit, so neither is pricier, whatever their price tags say.

cards.title: Two more numbers on the page
cards.body: Most quote pages show two more numbers. The *52-week high and low* are the highest and lowest prices of the past year. *Dividend yield* is the cash the shop pays you each year, as a percent of the price.
cards.simpler: Most quote pages also show two more numbers. The 52-week high and low are the past year's top and bottom prices. Dividend yield is the cash the shop pays out each year, as a percent of the price.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **A share price on its own tells you almost nothing.** It's the cost of one slice. Market cap tells you how big the shop is, and P/E tells you how many years of profit you're paying for.
cards.simpler: **A share price on its own tells you almost nothing.** It's the cost of one slice. Market cap tells you how big the whole shop is. P/E tells you how many years of profit you're paying for.

cards.body:
Open your broker app or the NSE website and look up any Nifty 50 company. Find its market cap and P/E. Then look up a second company. Which shop is bigger, and which has the higher P/E?

Tomorrow: how to buy all 50 big shops at once, for a tiny yearly fee.
cards.simpler: Open your broker app or the NSE website. Look up any company in the Nifty 50, the group of 50 big shops. Find **its market cap and its P/E**. Then do the same for a second company. Now compare the two. Which shop is bigger? Which one has the higher P/E, meaning you pay for more years of its profit? Tomorrow, you'll see how to buy all 50 big shops at once, for a tiny fee each year.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now look at a quote page and say whether a company is large or small, and whether it's priced high or low against its profit.

dubious_claims: 'The ₹3,000 slice is the cheaper buy' goes too far. A lower P/E means cheaper compared with profit, not automatically a better buy, because growth and risk also matter. 'Cheaper against its profit' is safer.
'Paid for the shop's profits until about 2116' only works if the reader is in 2026, and it assumes profit never changes. The joke is fine but the date will go out of date.
repairedFrom.why: Card 6 is about 120 words, right at the limit. It fits P/E, the 52-week high and low, and dividend yield into one card. No exercise tests the last two, so they look tacked on to reach 'five numbers' and pull the chapter away from one idea.
repairedFrom.fix: Remove the 52-week and dividend sentences from card 6 and put them on a short card of their own, or rename the chapter around price, market cap and P/E. Also move the 'Tomorrow: how to buy all 50 big shops at once' line so it comes after the try card and closes the chapter.
